poster.title: The Wind Rises
poster.alt: The Wind Rises: blue sky and clouds above a man in a lavender jacket, with black calligraphy and a pink Japanese title.
poster.blurb: An expanse of blue. A human gesture. A vivid pink title. Eighteen ways into one image.

studyData.intro: Follow a word, a colour, a gesture. There is a whole world inside this image.

regions.label: The studio signs the image
regions.summary: A small mark brings a whole set of expectations.

sections.heading: A Studio Ghibli film
sections.body: 作品 means a work or creation; here, “film” is the natural English choice.
sections.japanese: スタジオジブリ作品 / STUDIO GHIBLI
sections.translation: A Studio Ghibli film / Studio Ghibli

sources.note: The upper-left signature reads スタジオジブリ作品 / STUDIO GHIBLI. The English rendering here translates that visible inscription.

sections.heading: Recognition without taking over
sections.body: White lettering stands out on dark blue. Its modest size leaves the illustration dominant while letting an informed viewer recognise the studio.

sections.heading: Authorship is also a signal
sections.body: A studio name can help viewers decide what to expect. The poster itself does not tell us how much this recognition affected ticket sales.

regions.question: What do you expect before reading the title, simply from seeing this name?

regions.label: The brush-written call to live
regions.summary: Four forceful syllables make the sky speak.

sections.heading: A compact statement of resolve
sections.body: The subject is unstated. This shortened literary expression means “must live”; the longer English rendering conveys persistence.
sections.translation: We must live. / We must go on living.

sources.note: The poster supplies the exact wording 生きねば。 The English wording is a translation; the Japanese leaves its subject unstated.

sections.heading: A hand, not an identified font
sections.body: Producer Toshio Suzuki wrote the slogan. Thick and thin strokes, rough edges and uneven spacing preserve the movement of the brush.

sources.note: Miyazaki identifies Suzuki as the writer of 生きねば and comments on its size relative to the title.
The contemporary announcement also credits the slogan to Suzuki. These accounts establish authorship, rather than a font name.

sections.heading: Resolve above a hopeful scene
sections.body: The words can make the beautiful sky feel less carefree: living becomes something to undertake with determination. This is a reading of the juxtaposition.

regions.question: Would the message feel equally urgent in a perfectly even sans-serif?

regions.label: Two names, two kinds of legacy
regions.summary: The two names reveal the film’s unusual starting point.

sections.heading: Read down, then across
sections.body: Start with the right-hand column, then move to the left. と links the names; 敬意を込めて means “with respect.”
sections.japanese: 堀越二郎と堀辰雄に 敬意を込めて。
sections.reading: Horikoshi Jirō to Hori Tatsuo ni, keii o komete.
sections.translation: In tribute to Jirō Horikoshi and Tatsuo Hori.

sources.note: The two vertical columns contain the names Horikoshi Jirō and Hori Tatsuo and the expression 敬意を込めて.
The reading order follows the standard convention for vertical Japanese: down each column, moving from the right-hand column to the left.

sections.heading: Two lives, one fictional protagonist
sections.body: Ghibli says Miyazaki combined elements of aircraft designer Horikoshi and writer Hori. The result is imaginative historical storytelling, rather than a literal biography.

sources.note: Ghibli explicitly describes bringing Horikoshi and Hori together in one fictional Jirō. The protagonist should not be treated as a literal biography of either man.

sections.heading: A quieter inscription
sections.body: Fine, restrained lettering sits beside the much heavier slogan. The exact typeface cannot be identified reliably from this image.

regions.question: What changes when an aircraft story is dedicated to both an engineer and a writer?

regions.label: Flight, beauty and responsibility
regions.summary: A diagonal machine opens a question about making.

sections.heading: The picture extends beyond the sheet
sections.body: A wing runs off the left edge; pale surfaces separate from the blue; the blurred propeller suggests movement. The diagonal gives the otherwise vertical poster energy.

sections.heading: Beautiful design, difficult consequences
sections.body: Miyazaki’s proposal describes an engineer devoted to beautiful aircraft while warning that beauty can carry a cost.
sections.interpretation: This invites a question about responsibility for the uses of one’s work.
sections.note: This explorer does not identify the pictured aircraft as a particular model.

sources.note: The proposal links the pursuit of beautiful aircraft with the cost that beauty can carry. The question about responsibility is our reading, not a quoted statement of the poster’s intent.

regions.question: Does excellence in making something settle whether it ought to be made?

regions.label: Blue space to look into
regions.summary: The emptiest part does some of the most important work.

sections.heading: Room for the eye
sections.body: The broad blue field keeps the smaller forms legible. Openness can suggest possibility here, but blue has no single universal emotional meaning.
sections.note: Samples come from a JPEG, not original printing specifications.

sections.heading: History in living colour
sections.body: For the film, Miyazaki asked for beautiful skies and white clouds and rejected sepia treatment of period architecture.
sections.interpretation: This vivid poster is consistent with that direction; its precise intention is not documented.

sources.note: The visual direction calls for beautiful skies and white clouds and rejects sepia period architecture. This concerns the film; the connection to the poster is an interpretation.

regions.question: What becomes harder to notice if this open sky is filled with more objects?

regions.label: Clouds that make space
regions.summary: Soft forms give the aircraft a world to move through.

sections.heading: A cloud is more than white
sections.body: Blue-grey shadows and light edges create volume. Rounded forms contrast with straight wings and bridge the upper aircraft and lower figure.

sections.heading: Beauty is a selective view
sections.body: The expansive cloud can feel dreamlike. The poster offers one beautiful view of a story whose setting also includes disaster, illness and war; it cannot contain the whole story.

regions.question: What happens to the sense of distance if you mentally remove the cloud?

regions.label: A human point of entry
regions.summary: A calm face draws us into an unsettled world.

sections.heading: Looking up rather than out
sections.body: Warm skin and dark contours stand out against cool surroundings. The raised chin directs attention upwards. Curiosity or anticipation are plausible readings, not certain emotions.

sections.heading: Modern ambitions, difficult conditions
sections.body: The film moves from Taishō Japan into early Shōwa. Its setting includes the 1923 Great Kantō Earthquake, economic depression, tuberculosis and Japan’s movement towards war.

sources.note: The official synopsis places Jirō’s story in Taishō and early Shōwa Japan, amid hardship and upheaval.
The production notes describe the earthquake, depression, illness and approach of war that frame the story.

regions.question: Would a direct gaze at you tell a different story from this upward gaze?

regions.label: Another way to follow a dream
regions.summary: The spectacles connect appearance with a life choice.

sections.heading: A recognisable rhythm
sections.body: Two dark circular frames give the face a strong identifying feature. Their weight keeps them visible even when the whole poster is small.

sections.heading: From flying to designing
sections.body: The official synopsis says Jirō’s nearsightedness prevents him becoming a pilot, so he pursues aircraft design.
sections.interpretation: Connecting the visible glasses with this theme is an interpretive step.

sources.note: The synopsis in the production notes links Jirō’s nearsightedness to his choice of aircraft design rather than piloting. Reading the pictured glasses as a sign of that choice is interpretive.

regions.question: When one path closes, what other role might still serve the same ambition?

regions.label: Making the wind visible
regions.summary: A hand and a brim can suggest what we cannot see.

sections.heading: A frame for the face
sections.body: The broad curved hat frames the dark hair. The raised arm and hand near the brim can be read as steadying it outdoors.

sections.heading: A gesture with a possible story
sections.body: That reading makes wind visible through its effect on a person. It connects pose, sky and title. The picture alone does not establish an exact hat model or its owner’s social class.

regions.question: How can a still picture suggest a force you cannot actually see?

regions.label: The soft foreground silhouette
regions.summary: Muted clothing leaves room for a vivid title.

sections.heading: Lavender, then a blue echo
sections.body: The pale jacket creates a large, gentle foreground shape. The blue tie repeats the sky within the figure and gives the pink title a quieter background.

sections.heading: Dressed for a modern professional life?
sections.body: Jacket, collared shirt and tie make the figure look formally dressed. A professional identity is a plausible reading in this story; clothing alone cannot establish occupation, wealth or rank.

regions.question: How would the image change if the jacket were saturated red?

regions.label: A name as a promise
regions.summary: The creator’s name becomes part of the invitation.

sections.heading: A film by Hayao Miyazaki
sections.body: 監督 means director; 作品 means work. Ghibli also credits Miyazaki with the original work and screenplay.
sections.japanese: 宮崎 駿 監督作品
sections.translation: A film directed by Hayao Miyazaki.

sources.note: The official record credits Miyazaki with the original work, screenplay and direction, supporting the authorship described in this note.

sections.heading: Compact and authoritative
sections.body: Heavy Gothic/sans-serif-style Japanese lettering contrasts with the irregular title. Its position makes authorship prominent. The exact font family is unidentified.

sections.heading: A creator can be a recognition cue
sections.body: For viewers familiar with his work, a director’s name may carry expectations before they know the plot. This is a marketing reading, not a measured sales effect.

regions.question: When is a creator’s name as persuasive as the story being advertised?

regions.label: The title rises in pink
regions.summary: Literary words become the poster’s boldest colour accent.

sections.heading: The wind has risen
sections.body: 風 means wind. Here ぬ is a classical completion ending, giving the title an older literary register.
sections.translation: The Wind Rises; more literally, “The wind has risen.”

sources.note: Ghibli’s record confirms the Japanese film title, 風立ちぬ.
PDF page 38 explains the completion ending ぬ: the wind has arisen and continues. This supports the literal reading, rather than treating ぬ as a negative.

sections.heading: Custom lettering with a vivid accent
sections.body: Miyazaki wrote the title lettering. Irregular contours and a dark outline hold the large pink forms together over clothing and cloud.
sections.note: Pink alone does not establish an intended audience’s gender.

sources.note: Miyazaki says he wrote 風立ちぬ. The transcript establishes who made the lettering, not why pink was chosen.
The April 2013 report corroborates Miyazaki’s title-lettering credit. The colour and outline described above can be inspected in the poster itself.

sections.heading: A phrase travels between art forms
sections.body: The title comes from Hori’s novel. Miyazaki’s proposal traces the phrase to Hori’s Japanese rendering of a line by French poet Paul Valéry.

sources.note: The proposal connects the title to Hori’s novel and Hori’s rendering of Valéry’s line, establishing its literary route into the film.

regions.question: Where does your eye go first: the title, the face or the calligraphy?

regions.label: The voices behind the faces
regions.summary: The smallest names make human performance visible.

sections.heading: The voice performers
sections.body: These are people’s names, read left to right. The full transcription appears in the transcript.
sections.japanese: 庵野秀明・瀧本美織・西島秀俊 …
sections.translation: Hideaki Anno · Miori Takimoto · Hidetoshi Nishijima …

sources.note: The official credits pair Hideaki Anno with Jirō, Miori Takimoto with Nahoko and Hidetoshi Nishijima with Honjō.

sections.heading: A second reading speed
sections.body: The compressed horizontal line rewards a closer look. Image and title work at a distance; these names ask the viewer to slow down.

regions.question: Whose labour is visible in large letters, and whose appears only in small print?

regions.label: The poster hints at a soundtrack
regions.summary: One short line connects image, music and publishing.

sections.heading: Music and theme song
sections.body: サントラ abbreviates “soundtrack.” The same line credits Miyazaki’s original work, screenplay and direction, and its magazine serialisation.
sections.japanese: 音楽／久石 譲　主題歌／「ひこうき雲」荒井由実
sections.translation: Music: Joe Hisaishi. Theme song: “Hikōki-gumo” (“Vapor Trail” or “Contrail”) by Yumi Arai.

sources.note: The credits name Joe Hisaishi for music and Yumi Arai’s “Hikōki-gumo” as the theme song. They also list Miyazaki’s roles and the magazine serialisation.

sections.heading: Several media meet in one line
sections.body: The printed credits connect a film with Model Graphix magazine, Tokuma Japan Communications and EMI Records Japan. They reveal a broader creative and commercial network without disclosing its contracts.

sources.note: Model Graphix, Tokuma Japan Communications and EMI Records Japan are printed in the creative-credit line. The image does not disclose their contractual arrangements.

regions.question: How much can a silent poster make you anticipate a film’s sound?

regions.label: A coalition behind the film
regions.summary: A single artwork carries many organisations.

sections.heading: Made in association with…
sections.body: The partner line names Studio Ghibli, Nippon Television, Dentsu, Hakuhodo DYMP, Disney, Mitsubishi Corporation, Toho and KDDI.
sections.translation: A film made in association with the listed companies.

sources.note: The industry record lists the eight production partners named in this note, providing a check against the compact company-credit line.

sections.heading: Different jobs in the same ecosystem
sections.body: UNIJAPAN identifies Studio Ghibli as the production studio and Toho as Japanese distributor. A company credit does not disclose its investment, revenue share or creative control.

sources.note: The record distinguishes Studio Ghibli as production studio and Toho as Japanese distributor. It provides no basis for assigning investment shares or creative control.

regions.question: What expertise is needed between a creative idea and a cinema release?

regions.label: From cinema to the phone shop
regions.summary: A tiny credit opens a much bigger marketing story.

sections.heading: Sponsor, supporters, distributor
sections.body: These labels distinguish the roles printed on the poster.
sections.japanese: 特別協賛／KDDI　特別協力／ローソン、読売新聞　配給／東宝
sections.translation: Special sponsor: KDDI. Special cooperation: Lawson and Yomiuri Shimbun. Distributor: Toho.

sources.note: The lower credit line separates special sponsorship, special cooperation and distribution. These are the roles printed on this poster.

sections.heading: A real 2013 campaign
sections.body: KDDI’s au loves Ghibli campaign collected fan letters, offered special videos and gave limited folding-fan gifts to new au Smart Pass subscribers. The credit connects to activity beyond the cinema.
sections.note: This was a historical campaign, not a current offer.

sources.note: KDDI announced a July–September 2013 campaign with fan letters and special videos. Limited folding fans were offered to eligible new au Smart Pass subscribers while stocks lasted.

regions.question: What might a film studio and a telecom company each gain from a partnership?

regions.label: An invitation with a date
regions.summary: The bottom line tells the viewer what to do next.

sections.heading: Saturday, 20 July
sections.body: The date is the Japanese cinema opening in 2013. 全国 means nationwide; ロードショー here announces a theatrical release.
sections.translation: In cinemas nationwide from Saturday, 20 July.

sources.note: The official release date is 20 July 2013. It supplies the year omitted from the poster’s opening-day line.

sections.heading: A practical answer after an emotional image
sections.body: The imagery attracts attention; the release line supplies a time and place to act. Its bold, orderly type makes the information quick to retrieve.

regions.question: How does an advertisement turn curiosity into a real-world action?

regions.label: The poster’s small-print edge
regions.summary: Addresses, ownership and the limits of a small image.

sections.heading: Website and copyright
sections.body: The website is transcribed as printed. Nibariki is a company name; the letter sequence is retained unchanged.
sections.japanese: kazetachinu.jp　©2013 二馬力・GNDHDDTK　東宝

sources.note: The web address and copyright sequence are transcribed from the original image. The printed address is historical; it is not a recommendation to visit it today.
TOHO identifies its reprint as the second theatrical poster and retains the original 2013 copyright credit, providing an official cross-check.

sections.heading: Two details remain unresolved
sections.body: Only グループ (“group”) is securely readable in the caption beside the pig-shaped mark. The fine details and number of the far-right certification mark remain unclear.
sections.note: A sharper original is needed. Missing characters have not been supplied by guesswork.

sections.heading: A route beyond the paper
sections.body: The printed web address gives viewers a route from a physical poster to further film information. It makes the poster an entry point into a larger promotion.

regions.question: When should a careful reader record uncertainty instead of completing a pattern?

sources.title: The original Japanese theatrical poster, version 2
sources.summary: The reproduced poster is the visual record for its Japanese wording, credits, colours and layout. English translations and visual readings are supplied by Poster Atlas.

sources.title: TOHO: official reprint of the second theatrical poster
sources.summary: TOHO describes this product as a reprint of the second theatrical poster. Its listing helps identify the poster edition and the original 2013 copyright line.

sources.title: Studio Ghibli: The Wind Rises
sources.summary: Ghibli’s film record lists the principal creators, cast, running time, Japanese distributor and 20 July 2013 opening date.

sources.title: Studio Ghibli: July 2013 studio newsletter
sources.summary: The studio’s July 2013 newsletter explains how Miyazaki brought together aircraft designer Jirō Horikoshi and writer Tatsuo Hori in a fictional protagonist.

sources.title: Disney Japan: synopsis and complete credits
sources.summary: Disney Japan provides the film’s synopsis and credits, including character–performer pairings, music, theme song and publishing credits.

sources.title: Miyazaki’s project proposal, reproduced on the theatrical flyer (page 2)
sources.summary: Miyazaki’s proposal discusses beautiful aircraft, the costs of that pursuit, the film’s literary roots and its intended visual world. It does not document every choice in this poster.

sources.title: Studio Ghibli / Wild Bunch production notes, reproduced by SciFi Japan
sources.summary: These studio production notes describe Jirō’s nearsightedness, his path into aircraft design and the film’s historical setting. They are a historical publicity document.

sources.title: UNIJAPAN: The Wind Rises production and distribution record
sources.summary: UNIJAPAN identifies the production partners, production studio and Japanese distributor. These credits do not disclose investment shares or creative control.

sources.title: KDDI: au loves Ghibli campaign, 4 July 2013
sources.summary: KDDI’s July 2013 announcement describes the au loves Ghibli campaign, including fan letters, special videos and limited folding-fan gifts. It is a historical promotion.

sources.title: Miyazaki’s 2013 press conference: title lettering and Suzuki’s slogan
sources.summary: In the September 2013 press-conference transcript, Miyazaki says he wrote the title and Toshio Suzuki wrote the larger “must live” slogan.

sources.title: CinemaToday: announcement and lettering credits, April 2013
sources.summary: This April 2013 report independently records the lettering credits: the title by Hayao Miyazaki and the slogan by Toshio Suzuki.

sources.title: Otemae University: the classical grammar of 風立ちぬ
sources.summary: The teaching material explains that ぬ in 風立ちぬ marks completion in classical Japanese. Here it is not a negative ending; see PDF page 38.

sources.title: W3C: Requirements for Japanese Text Layout
sources.summary: W3C describes Japanese text-layout conventions, including vertical columns read top to bottom and from right to left. It does not identify the poster’s typefaces.

palette.name: Deep sky blue
palette.role: An open field around the words and aircraft.

palette.name: Pale lavender
palette.role: A soft foreground shape in the jacket.

palette.name: Cloud blue-white
palette.role: Light and volume within the cloud.

palette.name: Muted blue tie
palette.role: A link between figure and sky.

connections.label: Follow the gaze
connections.title: A face, a machine, a few words
connections.text: Follow Jirō’s upward gaze towards the aircraft and the calligraphy. Bring the poster together and see how that upward movement carries through the whole composition.

connections.label: Trace blue & pink
connections.title: Two colours hold the image apart
connections.text: The broad blue field and the bright pink title sit far apart in the flat image. Opening the stack makes their different roles visible; assembling it brings the contrast back into one field.

connections.label: Connect the words
connections.title: Two voices in one poster
connections.text: The compact black slogan and the expansive pink title differ in scale, placement and lettering. Watch them settle around the picture as you bring the layers together.

layers.label: Sky & open space
layers.description: The blue field gives the image its scale and makes the lighter forms easy to distinguish.

layers.label: Clouds & depth
layers.description: Light and shadow give the clouds volume. Notice the contrast between soft cloud forms and straight wings.

layers.label: Aircraft & motion
layers.description: The cropped wing and diagonal flight path bring motion into a still image.

layers.label: Portrait & clothing
layers.description: The face, raised arm and clothing bring a human scale to the expanse of sky.

layers.label: Upper lettering & logo
layers.description: The slogan, dedication and studio mark create a second way of reading the space above the figure.

layers.label: Title & small print
layers.description: A vivid title works from a distance; cast, music and production credits reward a closer look.
